What are the most mysterious undeciphered writing systems in history?
a: Several ancient scripts remain mysterious and undeciphered, challenging our understanding of past civilizations. The Voynich Manuscript, a 15th-century codex, contains an unknown script with bizarre botanical and astronomical illustrations that no cryptographer has been able to decode despite over a century of study. Linear A, used by the Minoan civilization on Crete from approximately 1800 to 1450 BCE, remains undeciphered despite being related to the known Linear B script. The Rongorongo script of Easter Island, consisting of intricate glyphs carved on wooden tablets, has resisted all attempts at decipherment, and researchers are unsure even of the underlying language. The Indus Valley script, found on seals and tablets from the Bronze Age Indus civilization (3300-1300 BCE), consists of over 400 distinct symbols that have not been linked to any known language. The Proto-Elamite script from ancient Iran, dating to around 3100 BCE, is another undeciphered writing system with over 160 signs. The Zapotec script from ancient Oaxaca, Mexico, consists of logograms and syllabic signs that remain largely undeciphered. The Pahlavi scripts, used in ancient Persia, are partially decipherable but contain many ambiguous characters. The Meroitic script of ancient Nubia, used to write the Meroitic language, has been partially decoded but the language itself remains poorly understood. Some researchers believe these scripts may represent lost languages, invented languages, or even non-linguistic symbolic systems. Others propose that they may be deciphered with the help of artificial intelligence and advanced statistical analysis, as was done with the Rosetta Stone for Egyptian hieroglyphs.
